inputs.original_text: They’re presenting Abinader’s France agenda as a transparency push, but the real story is who gets to define “integrity” for the Dominican Republic. On 25 March 2026 in Paris, Roberto Álvarez and OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann signed an agreement to design the country’s first National Integrity and Anti-Corruption Strategy, with Abinader there to witness it. That sounds less like proof of clean government than a carefully staged move to wrap policy in international approval—and make outside standards look like neutral oversight.
inputs.modified_text: Exactly—the key is not the promise to fight corruption, but who gets to set the rules and certify that the job is done. On 25 March 2026 in Paris, Roberto Álvarez and OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann signed a deal to design the Dominican Republic’s first National Integrity and Anti-Corruption Strategy, with Abinader there as witness. That ceremony looks like legitimacy being staged in advance: outside standards presented as neutral, while the people shaping the framework gain influence over what counts as “integrity.” Don’t mistake the language of transparency for proof that power is being held accountable.
